Direct HitProject record · built 2026-09-17

Direct Hit

Battleships, except every hit is a real ship taking a real shell. Call a square, and if something is under it the board steps aside: a camera drops to the water beside the vessel you just found, the round comes in, and you watch the hull take it. The ship in the cutscene is the ship you hit, the hole is where along her length you hit her, and if that was her last square she goes down while you watch.

5Ships
12Scripts

2Commits
6Decisions

How the game got made

Pipeline

The rules were built and proven before anything was drawn, because everything visible is generated from one dictionary the rules hand over: which ship, how far along her hull, and whether she went down. If the cutscene ever disagrees with the board, the board is right.

  1. AskWhere the cutscenes come from, what to build it in, who the player plays against - put to Luqman before a line was written.01-idea.md, 06-decisions.md
  2. Rules firstThe board, the fleet and the computer gunner, proven with nothing drawn.scripts/board.gd, dev/checks/_rules.gd
  3. HullsFive models downloaded, measured, and corrected in a table rather than edited.scripts/ship_models.gd
  4. Stage itOcean, sky, camera, shell, fire and smoke - all generated from the result of the shot.scripts/cutscene.gd
  5. LookPhotographs at exact beats, read back and judged by eye.dev/looks/, dev/shots/
  6. CheckHeadless scenes that end in a verdict, including the leak a correct rule set cannot catch.dev/checks/
  7. Play and reviewLuqman plays and reports back; the notes record what was decided.log/, 06-decisions.md

Tools

Godot 4.7.2Engine. Everything is built in code, including the board and the cutscene, so every camera mark and explosion timing reads in one file.
GDScriptAll game logic, the rules apart from the staging.
SketchfabAll five hulls, CC Attribution, normalised at load by ship_models.gd.
sfx (Freesound)CC0 sound only, with every file's source recorded in assets/audio/freesound/SOURCES.md.
ffmpegOne conversion: this build of Godot has no FLAC importer and drops the file without saying so.
Knowledge baseThe project notes this page is built from, kept outside the repo.

What the player sees

Screens

Every screenshot on this page was taken by a scene that drives the game from outside and saves a frame, because the questions that matter here are visual ones. A ship sailing backwards has exactly the same bounding box as one sailing forwards.

The board

The chart is drawn rather than assembled from sprites, so it scales with the window and the burst on a hit never turns blurry. The title screen is the cutscene's own ocean, running live behind the words.

The fleet

Five real vessels, pulled from Sketchfab under CC Attribution and normalised at load rather than edited. Each is rebuilt to the same number of units per grid square, so a five-square carrier really is two and a half times a two-square destroyer. These are the photographs that caught the submarine sailing stern-first.

The moment the whole game exists for

The cutscene

Not a clip. The sea, the ship, the shell and the fire are generated live from the shot that was just scored, which is the only way the vessel on screen can be the vessel you hit and the hole can be where you hit her. A clip cannot know either. Any click skips it.

A hit she survives about three and a half seconds

A hit that finishes her about seven and a half seconds

The same shot on the smallest hull the framing has to hold at a quarter the length

01-idea.md · 6 sections

Idea

The idea as Luqman put it

"A battleships game, but whenever a player gets a hit, a cutscene of realistic ships getting hit appears." (2026-09-17)

What that turned into

The rules of Battleships are untouched — a 10x10 grid, a fleet of five, alternate shots, sink everything. Everything built on top of that serves one moment: the half second after a shot lands on something.

When it does, the board is replaced by open ocean. The vessel you found is there, under way, at the size she should be relative to the others. A shell arcives from off the bow, the hull takes it where you hit it, and fire and smoke come out of the hole. If that was her last square she rolls, settles and goes under while the camera stands off and watches.

The decision that shaped everything else

Four ways to make those clips were put to Luqman: render them in Blender, generate them with AI, use CC0 stock footage, or build them in the engine and play them live. He chose real time in-engine, which is the most demanding of the four and the only one that can be correct: a pre-rendered clip cannot know that you hit the carrier three squares back from the bow, so it can only ever show a generic explosion and hope.

Target users

SegmentNeedWhy they'd pick this
Anyone who already knows BattleshipsNo rules to learnThe rules are the ones they know; only the payoff is new
Two people with one laptopSomething to play togetherPass-the-device mode needs no second device and no network

Value / advantage

  • The cutscene is accurate, not decorative — it is driven by the same dictionary that scores the shot.
  • Five real, recognisable vessels rather than abstract blocks.
  • No network, no accounts, no second device.

Assumptions to validate

AssumptionHow to testStatus
The cutscene stays a reward and does not become an interruptionPlay a full match and count how often the skip is useduntested — needs Luqman at the keyboard
~3.5s for a hit and ~7.6s for a sinking are the right lengthsSame playtestuntested
The computer at ~51 shots a game is a fair opponentPlay itmeasured, not felt

02-planning.md · 3 sections

Planning

Scope of v1 (built 2026-09-17)

In:

  • 10x10 board, standard fleet of five (carrier 5, battleship 4, cruiser 3, submarine 3, destroyer 2), no touching rule — overlap forbidden, adjacency fine.
  • Manual placement with a turn key and a scatter button, or scatter the lot.
  • Two modes: against the computer, and pass-the-device for two people.
  • A real-time 3D cutscene on every hit, and a longer one on a sinking.
  • Sea, sky, sound.

Out, deliberately:

  • Online play. It needs the Supabase project that is already outstanding for auxetic-chess and bluff-show, and two people on one laptop is enough for v1.
  • Difficulty levels. There is one computer opponent and it plays properly.
  • Salvo, mines, aircraft and the other Battleships variants.
What is left
  1. A playtest. Nobody has played this with their hands. Every claim about how it feels — cutscene length, whether the skip gets used, whether the computer is fun to lose to — is unverified.
  2. An export. No macOS or Windows build yet. referee-for-fun's tools/build/make_dmg.sh is the pattern to copy.
  3. Polish caught in review but left alone: the debris read as dark dashes rather than torn metal, and there is no wake behind a moving ship.

The project record exists as of 2026-09-17 — docs/index.html, built by tools/docs/build_docs.py and published at https://claude.ai/artifact/7q8gjEU9rWY2EoYerGeZPP. It has to be rebuilt and republished to that same URL whenever anything about the game changes.

Risks
RiskWhy it mattersMitigation
The cutscene outstays its welcomeIt fires on roughly one shot in threeSkip on any click, already in; lengths are two constants at the top of cutscene.gd
The ocean is 360k verticesIt could drag on weaker machinesIt renders only during the cutscene and the title screen; disabled everywhere else
Five CC-BY hullsCredit is a licence condition, not a courtesyCREDITS.md, per-model ATTRIBUTION.md, and an assets check that fails if one goes missing

The one that matters. Three suites of checks pass, but a check can only say the game is correct. Whether a cutscene every third shot is a reward or a nuisance, and whether the computer is enjoyable to play, are questions only a person at the keyboard can answer.

Run it with:

06-decisions.md · 6 sections

Decisions

D-001 — The cutscene is built in the engine and played live (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman from four options put to him: render the clips in Blender, generate them with AI (OpenArt credits), use CC0 stock naval footage, or build them in the engine in real time.

Real time is the most demanding of the four and the only one that can be correct. A pre-rendered clip cannot know which of five vessels you hit, or where along her hull, so it can only ever show a generic explosion. Everything that makes the idea worth building — the right ship, the right hole, a sinking only when she actually sank — depends on the cutscene being generated from the result of the shot.

Cost: an ocean, a sky, a particle system and a camera rig had to be built, and the sea is 360k vertices. It is rendered only during a cutscene and behind the title screen.

D-002 — Godot 4, not the browser (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman. His last four games went to the browser, which is far easier to share, but real-time 3D of this kind is where Godot earns its place. The cost is distribution: people will download a build rather than click a link.

D-003 — Both modes, computer and pass-the-device (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman over either alone. Online play was offered and declined for v1; it would need the Supabase project still outstanding from auxetic-chess and bluff-show.

D-004 — The board hands the cutscene one dictionary, and nothing else

Board.fire() returns which ship, how far along her hull, whether she sank. That dictionary is the only thing the cutscene is told. The cutscene decides nothing; if it ever disagrees with the board, the board is right. This is what makes it possible to check the rules with nothing drawn and still trust what is drawn.

D-005 — Models are corrected in a table, not in the files

The five hulls are left exactly as downloaded, and the scale, heading and waterline corrections live in ShipModels.TABLE. Editing the .glb files would have meant redoing that work every time a model is swapped, and would have hidden the corrections inside binary assets where nobody could read them.

D-006 — The view stays with the player against the computer

An early version let the on-screen viewpoint follow whoever's turn it was, which is right for two people sharing a device and badly wrong against the computer: it put the computer's own fleet face up on the player's chart every time it took a turn. The viewpoint now follows the device only when the device actually changes hands. dev/checks/_flow.gd tests this specifically.

04-methods.md · 6 sections

Methods

Normalising a downloaded hull

Five models from Sketchfab arrived in five different units and headings: the battleship 23 units long down X, the destroyer 0.16 down Z, the submarine 1476 down Z. Rather than editing the downloaded files — work that would have to be redone the moment one is replaced — each is left untouched and the corrections live in a table in scripts/ship_models.gd: which axis the hull runs along, whether its bow points the wrong way, and how far up the hull the sea sits.

Every ship is then rebuilt to CELL_LENGTH units per grid square, so a 5-square carrier really is two and a half times a 2-square destroyer, and a hit on segment 3 of 5 lands three squares back from the bow.

One unit is about three metres. Wave sizes, particle sizes and camera distances are all written in that scale.

Measuring a model that is not in the tree yet

Godot refuses to give a global transform to a node outside the scene tree: it prints an error and hands back the identity, which silently measures a nested model as though every part of it sat at the origin. A hull has to be measured before it is added to anything, so ShipModels.measure() walks the transforms by hand instead of asking for global_transform.

Photographing the work instead of describing it

Numbers cannot answer visual questions — a ship sailing backwards has exactly the same bounding box as one sailing forwards. dev/looks/ holds scenes that drive the game from outside and save PNGs into dev/shots/:

SceneWhat it answers
_hullsIs every hull the right size, the right way round, floating at the right depth?
_cutsceneWhat does a hit actually look like, beat by beat?
_screensEvery screen the player passes through, menu first

This caught the submarine sailing stern-first, the fireball detached from the hull, particles the size of the ship, and a camera that followed a sinking ship under the water.

Gerstner waves, and the two ways to get them wrong

The sea is four Gerstner waves stacked. Two mistakes were made and both are worth remembering:

  1. The horizontal push must be tied to the wave's own amplitude (steepness * amplitude), never to steepness / wavenumber. Divide by the wavenumber and a short wave gets a sideways push larger than its own height, the surface folds through itself, and calm water renders as broken glass.
  2. The shortest wave must stay several mesh quads wide. Below about three quads per wavelength the mesh cannot hold the shape and the sea becomes crumpled foil that crawls as the camera moves. This, not artistic preference, sets the floor on how short the waves may be.

Ocean swell also runs roughly sixty times longer than it is tall. The first set of waves was three times too steep and every shot looked like a gale.

Checking a game that cannot be played by a machine

Three suites in dev/checks/, each printing numbers and exiting non-zero on failure:

  • _rules — placement, shots, sinking, and 300 full computer games.
  • _flow — drives the real screens: does the battle screen come up, does the computer's fleet stay hidden, does the device change hands correctly?
  • _assets — does every model, sound and shader the game names actually load, and is every CC-BY hull still credited?

Run them:

cd ~/Desktop/project/game/direct-hit G=/Applications/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot $G --headless --path . res://dev/checks/_rules.tscn --quit-after 2000 $G --path . res://dev/checks/_flow.tscn --quit-after 3000 $G --headless --path . res://dev/checks/_assets.tscn --quit-after 1000

_flow needs a window because it builds real Control nodes.

Two traps this project fell into

A check that prints "all passed" while its own script is crashing. A GDScript runtime error prints and carries on; a whole section of the rules check did nothing for one run while the summary still claimed success. Checks now prove the thing they are testing can even be constructed before testing it.

Godot dropping a file without saying so. This build has no FLAC importer. A downloaded .flac was ignored at import, ResourceLoader.exists() returned false at runtime, and the game would simply have had no splash sound. The asset check exists to turn that silence into a failure; the file was converted to .wav with ffmpeg.

Technique
  • Gerstner waves — the standard formulation where horizontal displacement is steepness x amplitude x cos(phase) and the normal is built from the summed k x amplitude terms. Getting this wrong folds the surface; see 04-methods.md.
  • Naval facts worth keeping straight: a warship's ensign flies at the stern, which is how each model's heading was confirmed from a photograph rather than from its bounding box.

log/ · 1 sessions

Session log

2026-09-17

What Luqman asked for

"Create a new game project. I want a battleships game but whenever a player get a hit, a cutscene of realistic ships getting hit appear."

Three questions, three answers

Before anything was built he was asked where the clips should come from, what to build it in, and who the player plays against. He chose real-time 3D in the engine, Godot 4, and both computer and pass-the-device. The first of those decided the whole shape of the project — see D-001.

What got built

  • The rules engine first, checked with nothing drawn: placement, shots, sinking, and a computer gunner that hunts on a checkerboard and follows a line once it has two hits. 300 games all finish, averaging 51.7 shots. Random guessing takes about 96; a good human plays around 45.
  • Five hulls pulled from Sketchfab and normalised at load rather than edited.
  • The cutscene: Gerstner ocean, cloud sky, a shell that arcs in, fire, smoke, spray, debris, and a separate longer sinking.
  • The board: a drawn naval chart, fleet pips, placement with a turn key, two modes, and a handover screen.
  • Sound, all CC0.
  • Three check suites, all passing.

What went wrong, and what it taught

Almost every real bug was invisible in the code and only appeared in a photograph:

  • The submarine sailed stern-first. A bounding box cannot tell you which end is the bow; the propeller in a render can.
  • The fireball burned in mid-air beside the ship, because it was parented to the world instead of the hull.
  • Particles were the size of the ship — a particle's scale multiplies its quad, so a 6-unit quad at scale 16 is a 96-unit puff.
  • The camera followed a sinking ship under the water, because it was hanging off the hull. It now rides its own rig at sea level.
  • The sea rendered as broken glass, twice, for two different reasons — both now written up in 04-methods.md because both are easy to repeat.
  • A check printed "all passed" while its own script was crashing.
  • Godot silently dropped a downloaded FLAC; this build has no FLAC importer.

And one bug found by reading rather than looking: against the computer, the viewpoint followed whoever's turn it was, which would have shown the player the computer's entire fleet every time it fired. There is now a check for exactly that.

Where it stands

Playable end to end in both modes, all checks green — and never once played by hand. That is M6 and it is the next thing that matters. No export, no project record yet.

dev/checks and dev/looks, from each scene's own header

Checks and looks

A check runs and ends in a verdict. A look takes screenshots for a person to judge. Both are scenes under res://dev/. Between them they caught a submarine sailing stern-first, a fireball burning in mid-air, particles bigger than the ship, a camera that followed a sinking vessel under the water, and the computer's own fleet appearing face up on the player's chart.
